A similar correlation occurred in the 25-34 age group (a contingent that accounts for another five million voters). However, this pattern is maintained, intensified, in the CIS survey of July: the ultraderecha has a 13-point lead over the PP in the 18-24 age group, and more than six points in the next age group (25-34 years). The mutation of the ideological youth in Spain has no precedents. With the country just out of the dictatorship, young people leaned clearly to the left (and their location on the ideological scale reflected this, as they now sit one point to the right). Even in the early 90s, the percentage of young people under 35 who supported the PSOE or more left-wing forces doubled or even tripled the rate of adhesions to the right. The data from last May provides clues about the causes of this change. If the declared voting intention is segregated by sex, the result is very eloquent: among men aged 18-24, Vox outperforms the PP by almost eleven points (and seven in the 25-34 age group). However, among young women, it is the Partido Popular that outperforms the ultras: by 12 points in the 18-24 age group, and seven in the 25-34 age group. In short, the ultraderechization of young men has something of an egoistic rebellion against the advance of gender parity. Nevertheless, Spain is not an exceptional case. Other Western countries are experiencing a sustained rise in extreme right-wing parties with the decisive support of new generations. The recent Polish presidential elections are a good example: the ultra-candidate clearly won among those under 40 (and with a greater advantage among men). And something similar occurred in the German legislative elections, although here the young people radicalized towards the two extremes (AfD, to the right, and Die Linke, to the left). Of course, there are exceptions. In the Canadian legislative elections, the Liberal Party (center-left) won over the Conservative Party (close to Trump) thanks to the vote of those under 35 (and especially women). In contrast, the age group between 35 and 54 leaned towards the conservatives. However, unlike what happens not only on the other side of the Atlantic, in the Spanish case, the low level of education still does not play decisively in favor of the ultraderecha, which is residual among those who barely went to school (46% of them vote for the PSOE). And although Vox is also marginal among the working class, it is starting to have presence among the poorest.

Forecasters generally agree that Vox has experienced a rapid and unprecedented surge in voting intention among 18-24-year-olds in Spain, currently polling at or around the critical 27% threshold according to the latest 40dB survey. This rise is attributed to a broader rightward ideological shift among Spanish youth, effective digital and social media strategies by Vox, and resonance with economic and cultural grievances (especially among young men). Many experts note that this trend mirrors broader European patterns (as seen with AfD in Germany and RN in France), further supporting the plausibility of continued growth.

However, nearly all experts emphasize structural headwinds that might prevent Vox from definitively surpassing 27%: high abstention rates (youth are the most likely cohort to abstain from voting), a pronounced gender split (young women remain mostly left-leaning), and the entry or strength of alternative far-right/populist parties (such as Alvise or Aliança Catalana), which could fragment the radical right vote. Methodological factors, such as survey volatility and demographic weighting, also introduce uncertainty, making even minor fluctuations (due to chance) potentially decisive. Some caution that, while Vox is leading and the trend is still upward, recent polling appears to plateau, and the historical base rate for sudden post-peak surges is low unless driven by a major event or shock. 

Probabilities provided by experts range from around 33% (seeing a plateau and volatility as major barriers) to as high as 68% (viewing the persistent trend, social media strength, and European parallels as tailwinds likely to produce at least a marginal increase over 27%). Several experts cluster just above or just below even odds, reflecting genuine uncertainty rooted in competing structural forces: momentum, digital outreach, youth anomie, gender polarity, abstention, and potential vote splitting.

In summary, the consensus is that Vox surpassing 27% among young Spaniards by the end of 2025 is plausible and somewhat more likely than not—but far from certain. The outcome hinges on whether upward momentum and digital mobilization can outweigh abstention, gender limits, and competition. A polling result just above the threshold is entirely possible, but so is a stall or minor drop, with most forecasts between 40% and 68% probability of a 'Yes' outcome, and the median probability estimate slightly above 50%.
